subject: Problems with GOF and unreasonable predictions in gdistsamp

messages.author: 9650baa7f9da9041
messages.subject: Problems with GOF and unreasonable predictions in gdistsamp
parts:
Hi all,

 

I’ve been trying to figure out how to interpret density predicted in gdistsamp, but I think I’m doing something wrong. I’ve read several posts in the forum, but as this is still unclear I hope that someone can help me.



I’m analysing data for a songbird species across 53 survey sites; all sites were visited 3 times. I collected exact distance data in the field, but as required for gdistsamp I binned my data in 10m intervals and truncated data at 60 m as detection fell substantially after 60 m. I first ran constant models to choose the best mixture, and start building my models first adding habitat covariates affecting phi and p. The best model was the one where abundance of small trees (DBH 1-15 cm) negatively affects phi, which makes sense as this species forage on the canopy and places with small trees might be visited, but they probably spend less time in those areas.


I then, kept the covariate affecting phi (small trees) in subsequent models and start modelling covariates for lambda. After model selection I ended up with some competitive models (within 2 AIC), and my first problem is that only one of them pass the freemanTukey GOF test, but they all pass Chi-square test. Can I still keep those models?


But my main problem is with predict. One of the models included in the output attached contains 2 habitat covariates affecting abundance, they make ecological sense, but the results that I obtained from predict are really high for this species, so I’m wondering if I missed a step in the modelling process. I really appreciate if someone can help me with this.


Thank you,

 

Fernanda Alves.

messages.author: b655697c64cc729d
messages.subject: Re: Problems with GOF and unreasonable predictions in gdistsamp
parts:
I have run into similar problems with complex designs (ie., gdistsamp). You're fitted model has very low availability which results in an inflated abundance estimate. Have you considered trying distsamp and using your survey period (1 of 3) with the most detections? This will likely give a more reasonable abundance estimate but won't include variables causing variation in phi. 
Myles

messages.subject: Re: Problems with GOF and unreasonable predictions in gdistsamp
parts:
Hi Fernanda/Miles,

This may have changed in more recent versions or I may be terribly misinterpreting this, but just looking at the source code for gdistsamp, the density output associated with gdistsamp (or presumably any of the generalized models?) is simply lambda/area. I think that maybe in the context of the model as originally described (with availability corresponding to movement on to the plot/deciding to sing), density is something closer to (lamda*phi)/area.  Does about 1.5 birds per unit area sound more realistic? That's what I get from the intercept-only derivation.

Cheers,

John

Thank you Myles and John,

I still believe that gdistsamp is the best option for my analysis, because the fact that availability is being affected by small trees make sense, as birds probably use those areas, but don't stay there long.  So, John if density is (lambda*phi)/area as you said, which figures did you use to come up with 1.5 birds per unit area (and by unit area do you mean area in the 60 m radius surveyed (1.3 ha)?). And yes that sounds more realistic, but how do I get the predictions for the different levels of the covariates affecting lambda, I'd like to have something similar to the plot I have in the htm file I attached, but I'm not sure how to predict it, when there is also a covariate affecting phi in the model. 

Cheers,

Fernanda.

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Problems with GOF and unreasonable predictions in gdistsamp
parts:
Hi Fernanda,

I got the 1.5 number as exp(3.39)*inv.logit(-2.9): intercept-only lambda*intercept-only phi. By unit area, I guess per hectare given that it is the unitsOut argument? If availability is mostly impacted by movement (as opposed to something else like not singing), it seems to suggest that the plot size is quite a bit smaller than the intrinsic space a single bird might use: the effective area being sampled is much larger than the plots. The original paper (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/10-2433.1/pdf) goes into much more detail, but one pertinent part is this: 'Under temporary emigration, some members of the superpopulation will have activity centers outside of the plot; therefore, it would appear as though density (D) estimation would not be possible because the effective plot area (Ae) is unknown and larger than the actual plot area (A). However, because our model only assumes that plots are closed during the sampling occasion, not among sampling occasions, density can be estimated by D = (Lambda-hat*Phi-hat)/A." 

In terms of plotting predictions, I think it'd pry be pretty straight-forward to plot a derivation of E[density] by multiplying E[lambda] * E[phi]. The CI might be a little tougher.

Cheers,

John
